entries.name: Parks & Recreation Edition
entries.aff: Designed for the needs of municipal parks and recreation departments and organisations like them. This platform has NO affiliation with, endorsement from, partnership with, or contact of any kind with the National Recreation and Park Association, any city or county parks department, or any recreation authority. Nothing here is authorised by them and nothing should be represented as theirs.
entries.thesis: A parks department is not a youth agency that happens to own fields. It is a public works operation that also runs programmes: it holds the pool, the gym, the diamonds and the shelter, it answers to a city budget written in facility terms, and its programme staff are often seasonal, hired in April and gone in September. Nothing here assumes a year-round youth worker, a curriculum budget, or a room that is not also booked for something else at six. What a parks department actually has that nobody else does is space, water, ground and the legal right to let anybody in — and this edition is built on those four assets rather than on staff it does not have.
needs: Seasonal staff, hired in April
Most programme staff are eighteen to twenty-two, employed for one summer, trained in three days. Every session is written for them and no session assumes a returning adult.
The facility is the programme
The pool, the gym, the field and the shelter are the department’s real assets. Sessions are authored to the space rather than to a subject.
Booked at six for something else
No session may leave equipment out, occupy a room past its slot, or depend on a wall.
Registration exists but drop-in is the reality
Some programmes take enrolment; open gym and the pool do not. Both shapes are authored.
All ages, including seniors
A parks department serves eighty-year-olds and eight-year-olds on the same site on the same day. The bands include adults, not as an afterthought.
Fee-based and free run side by side
Some programmes must recover cost. Every session names whether it can run free and what it needs if it cannot.
Weather decides
Half of these programmes are outdoors. Every outdoor session names its indoor collapse.
Liability and water safety are the floor
Aquatics, contact and heights carry real risk and real law. Every session touching them names the certification actually required, and defers to it.
strands: The pool is the most valuable and most dangerous thing the department owns. Swimming as a survival skill, not a sport.
Fields, courts and the games people actually play on them, including the ones without leagues.
Trails, parks, weather, night sky, growing things. The city’s land, used deliberately.
The building on a rainy day

Older adults and all ages together

units.w: Learning to be calm and horizontal before any stroke, because drowning is a panic event before it is a skill gap.
Every child practises exiting from the deep end unaided, at the wall and at the ladder.

entries.name: Rural & Agricultural Youth Edition
entries.aff: Designed for the needs of rural school districts, extension offices, agricultural youth organisations and the communities they serve. This platform has NO affiliation with, endorsement from, partnership with, or contact of any kind with 4-H, the National FFA Organization, the Cooperative Extension System, USDA or any land-grant university. Nothing here uses their programme names, emblems or curricula, and nothing should be represented as theirs.
entries.thesis: Rural is not urban with fewer people. It is a different set of constraints: an hour each way on a bus, one adult who teaches four subjects, a seasonal calendar that pulls young people out of school for harvest because the family operation genuinely needs them, an economy where the best-paid local work is skilled and physical, and broadband that either is not there or is not affordable. The deficit framing that treats a rural young person as somebody to be prepared for leaving is both insulting and a policy failure, because it exports the talent that a place needs. This edition assumes the young person may stay, may leave, or may leave and come back, and that all three are legitimate. It is built for distance, seasonality and a community where everybody knows everybody, which is a safeguarding condition as much as a social one.
needs: Distance is the first constraint
An hour on a bus each way is normal. Nothing here requires attendance more than once a week, and every unit has an asynchronous route.
One adult teaches everything
The agriculture teacher is also the shop teacher, the club advisor and the bus driver. Sessions must not need a specialist.
The season overrides the calendar
Planting, calving and harvest pull young people out. The curriculum is authored so that missing three weeks in October is not failure.
Connectivity cannot be assumed
Every unit names a route that works with no home internet and a phone with a data cap.
Real work, young
Many young people here already do serious physical work. The programme treats that as competence, not as a risk to be managed.
Everybody knows everybody
Confidentiality is structurally harder. Every unit touching a personal matter names an out-of-county route.
The best jobs are skilled and local
Line work, welding, diesel, health care, agronomy. The economy strand is built from what is actually hiring within an hour.
Leaving is not the goal, and neither is staying
Every unit that touches the future presents staying, leaving and returning as three legitimate paths, without ranking them.
strands: What the operation actually requires, treated as skilled work rather than as chores.
Diesel, hydraulics, welding, electrical. The most transferable skills in a rural economy.
Business and the money in it
Margins, inputs, weather risk, and why a good year and a good farm are different things.
Distance, connection and the internet you do not have
Getting an education, a job and a life across an hour of road and a poor connection.
The future conversation, held honestly, without ranking the three answers.

refusals: No deficit framing

No use of any organisation’s programme names or emblems
Nothing here is 4-H, FFA or Extension material, and nothing may be presented as theirs.

entries.name: Military-Connected Families Edition
entries.aff: Designed for the needs of schools, youth programmes and families with a service-member parent. This platform has NO affiliation with, endorsement from, partnership with, or contact of any kind with the Department of Defense, DoDEA, any branch of the armed forces, any installation, or any military family organisation. Nothing here is authorised, cleared or endorsed by them, and nothing should be represented as theirs. This edition takes no position on any deployment, conflict or policy.
entries.thesis: A military-connected child changes school six to nine times before graduating, is routinely the newest person in the room, and lives on a calendar set by an institution that does not consult them. The two hard things are not what people assume. The first is transition: credits that do not transfer, a sport season joined in week eleven, an IEP that restarts, and the exhausting work of being new again. The second is ambiguous loss — a parent who is alive but absent, whose return date moves, and whose absence has no ritual and no sympathy card. Programmes for these families usually offer either patriotic ceremony or clinical referral, and most families need neither on a Tuesday. They need the ordinary thing done well: a school that can enrol you in a day, an adult who knows your name in week one, and somewhere to put the part of you that is waiting.
needs: You will be new again
A move every two to three years. Every unit is authored so that arriving mid-year is normal rather than remedial.
Credits and records must move fast
Transcripts, IEPs, immunisations and sport eligibility. The transition strand is administrative because that is where children actually get hurt.
The calendar belongs to somebody else
Deployment, training, field exercises and duty. Nothing here requires a parent to be present on a fixed date.
Ambiguous loss is the real condition
A parent alive, absent, and returning on a date that moves. Named plainly, without pathologising a normal response to an abnormal situation.
Reintegration is harder than departure
The return is often the hardest month of the cycle, and almost nothing is written for it.
Not every family lives on an installation
Most do not. Every unit works for a family in a civilian school with no installation nearby.
Guard and Reserve families are alone
Mobilised from a community with no other military families in it, which is the least-served case and is authored for directly.
This is not recruitment, and not politics
No unit promotes service, discourages it, or takes a position on any conflict. The programme serves the child in front of it.

Ambiguous loss, the moving date, communication, and the ordinary week in the middle of it.

refusals: No position on any conflict, deployment or policy
The programme serves the child in front of it and takes no view on why their parent is away.
No recruitment, and no discouragement

No disclosure of a family’s situation

No assumption of an installation

No ceremony in place of help

entries.name: Reentry & Justice-Involved Youth Edition
entries.aff: Designed for the needs of juvenile justice education programmes, detention and secure school staff, reentry providers, probation departments and the young people they work with. This platform has NO affiliation with, endorsement from, partnership with, or contact of any kind with any court, correctional agency, probation department or provider. Nothing here is legal advice, and nothing here is a risk assessment, a screening instrument or a supervision tool.
entries.thesis: Education inside a facility is usually a placeholder: hours logged, credits that do not transfer, and a young person released in March with nothing to enrol in. The evidence about what decides reentry is not mysterious — school or work within the first fortnight, documents in hand, a place to sleep, and at least one adult who was there before and is still there after. Almost none of that is education, which is exactly why an education product has to be honest about its own edges. This edition is built around continuity: the same curriculum shape inside and outside, credits that actually move, a plan written before release rather than after, and a hard refusal to produce anything that could function as a record, a score or a supervision instrument. A young person’s file should not grow because they took a class.
needs: Release dates move
Nothing may depend on completing a sequence. Every unit stands alone and everything partially done still counts.
Credits must transfer or the time was wasted
The single largest failure of education inside. Every unit is authored against a transferable credit shape.
The first fortnight decides it
School or work within fourteen days is the strongest lever anybody has. The plan is written before release, not after.
Inside and outside must be the same shape
A young person should recognise the curriculum on both sides of the door.
Staff are correctional first
The adult in the room may be a teacher, an officer, or both. Units name which adult can run them.
Wide skill range in one room
Two years to ten years of reading range in a single classroom is normal. Every unit has a non-reading route.
The record follows them
A criminal record shapes housing, work and school. The record strand is practical and refers all legal questions out.
Trauma is the baseline, not the exception
Universal design rather than screening: no unit requires disclosure, and none produces a psychological judgement.
strands: Credits, transcripts, enrolment and the diploma route that survives a move between systems.
What it is, who sees it, what can be sealed or expunged, and where to go — refers, never advises.
Documents, a bed, an appointment, an enrolment and a phone, in the fourteen days that decide the year.

refusals: No record, score or instrument
Nothing this programme produces may function as evidence, a risk score, a supervision note or anything that reaches a court. A young person’s file must not grow because they took a class.
No requirement to disclose or admit anything
No unit asks what a young person did, and participation never depends on saying.
No legal advice
Record, sealing, expungement and immigration questions name the free legal route and stop there, every time.
No screening or assessment
Trauma-responsive by universal design, never by instrument, because instruments create records and records follow people.
No participation reported as compliance
Nothing here is a condition of release, probation or privileges, and no attendance data is shared with supervision.
No outcome claimed
Zero young people have used this. No recidivism, employment or enrolment result is claimed and none may be inferred.
